title: Bread for the Road
description: Two tired disciples walk away from Jerusalem, and a stranger walks with them. They only recognize him when he breaks the bread.
content:
It is seven miles from Jerusalem to Emmaus. Long enough to tell the whole story twice, and long enough to get it wrong both times. Cleopas and his friend are not running away, exactly. They are going home, which is what people do when the thing they hoped for has ended.

And then a stranger falls into step beside them. He asks what they are talking about, and they stop walking. Luke says they stood still, looking sad. It is one of the most honest lines in the Bible.

Recognized at the table

The stranger explains the scriptures all the way home, and still they do not know him. It is only at the table, when he takes the bread, blesses it and breaks it, that their eyes are opened.

That is why we keep coming back to this table on Sunday mornings. Not because we have worked it all out on the road, but because this is where he keeps making himself known — in ordinary bread, handed from one tired person to another.

Were not our hearts burning within us while he was talking to us on the road?

This week, notice who is walking beside you. It may be the very person you have not recognized yet.
speaker: Rev. Anna Whitley

title: The Stranger at the Door
description: Abraham runs to meet three travelers in the heat of the day. What we owe the people who turn up unannounced.
content:
It is the hottest part of the day, and Abraham is sitting in the doorway of his tent. Three men appear. He does not wait to see who they are. He runs.

The story is famous because of what happens next — the promise of a son, Sarah laughing behind the tent flap. But I want to stay with the running. An old man, in the heat, hurrying to wash the feet of people he has never met.

Hospitality before explanation

Abraham does not ask for references. He offers water, shade and bread first, and the conversation comes later. The letter to the Hebrews remembers this: some have entertained angels without knowing it.

Our red doors are open most days of the week. Some who walk through them are looking for God, some for a restroom, some for a sandwich. We are asked to run to all of them the same way.
speaker: Rev. Anna Whitley

title: A Well in Samaria
description: Jesus asks a woman for a drink at noon, and a conversation nobody was supposed to have changes a whole town.
content:
Nobody draws water at noon. You go in the cool of the morning, with everyone else. Unless, of course, you would rather not be with everyone else.

So the woman comes alone, and finds a Jewish teacher sitting on the edge of the well, asking her for a drink. Every rule of the day said this conversation should not happen.

Being fully known

He tells her everything she has ever done, and somehow she runs back into town not ashamed but amazed. Come and see, she says. Being fully known, it turns out, is not the same as being condemned.

Whatever you would rather nobody knew, bring it to the well. He is already sitting there.
speaker: Deacon Marcus Hale

title: Consider the Lilies
description: On worry, the price of sparrows, and why Jesus sends anxious people outside to look at flowers.
content:
Jesus does not tell anxious people to try harder. He tells them to go outside. Look at the birds. Look at the wildflowers in the field, which do not spin or sew, and are dressed better than Solomon.

It is not a lecture. It is an invitation to notice that we are held in a larger care than our own planning.

Today's trouble

Each day has enough trouble of its own, he says, which is not quite a promise that there will be no trouble. It is a promise that we will not have to carry tomorrow's today.

This week, take ten minutes outside without your phone. Consider the lilies. Then come back and tell us what you saw.
speaker: Rev. Anna Whitley
